entries.topicDescription: Dynamic arrays and hash maps — Go's essential data structures.

tips.title: Maps are hash tables with simple syntax
tips.content:
Maps in Go are built-in hash tables: map[KeyType]ValueType.
Keys must be comparable (==), which includes strings, ints,
and structs with comparable fields.

Always initialize maps before use: either with make() or a
literal. Writing to a nil map panics. Reading from a nil or
missing key returns the zero value.

Use the two-value form (value, ok := m[key]) to distinguish
between a missing key and a key with a zero value. This is
essential for maps of booleans or integers.

Maps are not safe for concurrent access. Use sync.RWMutex
or sync.Map when multiple goroutines read and write the
same map.

tips.title: Generics make slice and map utilities type-safe
tips.content:
Before Go 1.18, utility functions for slices and maps
required interface{} or code generation. Generics let you
write them once with full type safety.

The standard library's 'slices' and 'maps' packages (Go 1.21+)
provide common operations: sorting, searching, filtering,
and comparing. Use them instead of writing your own.

Type constraints like 'comparable' and 'constraints.Ordered'
restrict type parameters to types that support specific
operations. This catches errors at compile time.

Generics shine for data structure utilities but aren't
needed everywhere. If a function works fine with a concrete
type, keep it simple — don't add generics just because
you can.

tips.title: Slices are references to arrays — understand the gotchas
tips.content:
A slice is a descriptor (pointer, length, capacity) that
references an underlying array. Multiple slices can share
the same array, which is efficient but can cause surprises.

When you append to a slice and it exceeds capacity, Go
allocates a new, larger array and copies data. The old
slice and new slice now point to different arrays.

Use make([]T, length, capacity) to preallocate when you
know the size. This avoids repeated allocations during
append loops and significantly improves performance.

The built-in copy() function safely copies between slices.
Use it when you need an independent copy that won't affect
the original.
